title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String
statement: `s` is made of lowercase English letters. One move deletes a pair of identical letters that stand next to each other, and the pieces on either side then join up. Keep making moves while any such pair exists, and return the string that is left when none remains (it may be empty). The final string is the same whichever pairs you choose along the way.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating the rule directly (find a pair, cut it out, rescan) can cost O(n²), because each cut may expose a new pair further left. Notice that a new pair can only form between the last surviving letter and the next incoming one. If we keep the surviving letters on a stack, the only letter an incoming one can cancel with is the top, so a single left-to-right pass is enough.

## Approach

1. Start with an empty `stack` of surviving letters.
2. For each letter `ch` of `s`:
   - if the top of `stack` equals `ch`, the two cancel, so pop the top;
   - otherwise push `ch`.
3. Join the letters left on `stack`, bottom to top, and return them.

## Example 1, step by step

For `s = "abbaca"`: `a` is pushed (`[a]`), `b` is pushed (`[a, b]`), the second `b` matches the top and pops it (`[a]`), the next `a` matches and pops (`[]`), `c` is pushed (`[c]`) and `a` is pushed (`[c, a]`). Joining gives `"ca"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each letter is pushed at most once and popped at most once.
- Space: O(n) for the stack in the worst case, when nothing cancels.

## Pitfalls

- An incoming letter that matches the top is not pushed at all; pushing it and then popping two would remove a letter too many.
- Three equal letters in a row leave one behind (`"aaa"` becomes `"a"`): the pair cancels and the third has nothing to match.
- Building the result with repeated string slicing is quadratic; collect letters in an array and join once.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `stack` | letters that have survived so far, in order |
| `ch` | the letter of `s` being processed |

narration.2: The stack holds the letters that have survived so far, in order.
narration.3: Read the string one letter at a time.
narration.4: Does the new letter equal the last surviving letter?
narration.5: Yes: the two form an adjacent pair, so remove the top and drop the new letter.
narration.7: No: the letter survives for now, so push it.
narration.10: The letters left on the stack, bottom to top, are the final string.
